query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy is rapidly quenched from a sufficiently high superheat at cooling rates exceeding 1×10^5 K/s, then the resulting amorphous structure will exhibit at least a twofold increase in critical casting thickness and a crystallization onset temperature higher by 20–30 K compared to a similar alloy processed at conventional (lower) cooling rates, provided oxygen contamination is minimized.
generation.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy prepared as a homogenized ingot under inert atmosphere.
generation.intervention: Applying an ultra-rapid melt-quenching technique (e.g., melt spinning or laser melt-pool quenching) at cooling rates above 10^5 K/s.
generation.conditions: Melt superheated above the liquidus temperature, with controlled and minimized oxygen levels, and ensuring uniform cooling across the sample cross-section to avoid partial crystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: Suppression of crystalline nucleation and promotion of high mixing entropy in the undercooled liquid.
generation.mechanism: Rapid quenching impedes diffusion-limited growth of nuclei, while phosphorus and multiple principal elements increase mixing entropy, further hindering crystallization and stabilizing the amorphous state.
generation.predicted_outcome: An amorphous alloy with a higher critical casting thickness (about twice that of conventional casting) and an elevated crystallization onset temperature by 20–30 K when compared to slower cooling, arc-cast samples of the same composition.
generation.baseline: Identical alloy composition processed by standard casting methods at cooling rates below ~10^4 K/s and no additional superheat control.
generation.boundary: If the cooling rate is insufficient, the melt superheat is not properly controlled, or oxygen contamination is high, the enhancement in glass formation and thermal stability will be reduced or absent.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements may vary with specific compositions, and the strong synergy between phosphorus content and other principal elements requires further confirmation across multiple alloy chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare two sets of ingots with the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex composition: one set processed via standard slow cooling and one set via the proposed ultra-rapid quenching from an elevated superheat in an inert environment.
measurements: X-ray diffraction and TEM to confirm amorphous vs. crystalline structure.
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to measure the onset of crystallization temperatures.
Critical casting thickness measurements to assess glass-forming ability.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapidly quenched samples fail to show higher critical thickness or exhibit no significant shift in crystallization onset temperature relative to the control samples, or if the quickly quenched samples partially crystallize due to nonuniform or insufficient cooling, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This study investigates the influence of cooling rates on the microstructure and phase transformations of the high-entropy alloy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20. The alloy was synthesized via arc melting and subjected to three cooling conditions: slow cooling (52 K/s), accelerated cooling after a short electric arc pulse (3018 K/s), and rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K/s) using the melt-spinning method. The microstructures were characterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The thermal properties and phase transformations were analyzed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermography. Slow cooling produced a complex crystalline microstructure, while accelerated cooling resulted in fewer phases. Rapid cooling yielded an amorphous structure, demonstrating that phosphorus and high mixing entropy enhance glass-forming ability. Phase transformations exhibited significant undercooling under accelerated cooling, with FCC phase crystallization shifting from 1706 K (slow cooling) to 1341 K, and eutectic crystallization from 1206 K to 960 K. The cooling rates were systematically varied, with slow cooling averaging approximately 52 K/s, accelerated cooling at 3018 K/s, and melt-spinning achieving rapid cooling rates in the range of 10⁵–10⁶ K/s. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy bulk metallic glasses (especially with Refs. PMC8911233 and PMC9023469) showed that combining multiple principal elements can enhance glass formation by broadening the atomic size distribution and boosting structural disorder, thereby raising the glass transition temperature and mechanical robustness. More recently (Ref. PMC11642357), introducing phosphorus into a CrMnFeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy revealed that accelerated cooling rates could amplify undercooling and extend the stability range of the amorphous phase. Yet, there remains incomplete consensus on how best to manipulate synthesis or thermal histories to simultaneously boost glass-forming ability and improve the thermal stability of these P-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
decision.unsolved: It is still uncertain which specific single intervention can most robustly and reproducibly enhance both glass-forming ability and amorphous thermal stability in P-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, without relying on introducing additional elements.
decision.lever: Implement an ultra-rapid melt-quenching approach (e.g., melt spinning or laser melt-pool quenching) at cooling rates above 105 K/s for a P-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy, while holding the melt at a sufficiently high superheat to reduce retention of crystalline seeds.
decision.why: Testable hypothesis: Employing an ultra-rapid quench from a carefully controlled superheat for a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will yield a markedly higher critical glass thickness (e.g., doubled relative to standard casting) and an elevated onset temperature for crystallization by at least 20–30 K, provided that oxygen contamination is minimized and the superheat is sufficiently above the liquidus. Prior work (e.g., PMC11642357) shows that higher cooling rates can generate deeper undercooling, which correlates with enhanced glass formation in P-containing high mixing-entropy alloys. The approach should fail (falsifying the hypothesis) if uniform quenching rates are not achieved across the sample volume, preventing a fully amorphous phase or improvements to thermal stability. A single casting trial, comparing standard arc melting/casting with the proposed ultra-rapid quench (and measuring critical thickness plus glass transition and crystallization temperatures via DSC), would confirm or refute the predicted gains in glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
